title: Metrics and Alerting Platform
prompt: Design an internal platform that collects numeric metrics from every service and host in the company, lets engineers graph them, and pages someone when a rule is broken.

clarify.q: How many hosts and containers, and roughly how many distinct series each?
clarify.why: Active series count, not hosts, drives memory, index size and cost. Labels like user id can multiply it by thousands.

clarify.q: How often is each series sampled: every 10 s, every minute?
clarify.why: The interval sets samples per second, which sizes the whole write path.

clarify.q: Do agents push to us, or do we scrape them?
clarify.why: Pulling gives us control of the rate and an easy 'target is down' signal. Pushing suits short-lived jobs and networks we cannot reach into.

clarify.q: How long must raw data be kept, and how long do people look back?
clarify.why: Retention by resolution decides storage size and whether we need downsampling.

clarify.q: How fast must an alert fire after the condition starts?
clarify.why: Under a minute means alerts evaluate on recent in-memory data, not on files written to storage.

clarify.q: Are logs and traces in scope?
clarify.why: They have different shapes (text, spans) and different storage. Keeping only numbers in scope keeps the design focused.

functional: Ingest samples (name, labels, timestamp, value) from agents on every host.
Query a series or an aggregate across label filters over any time range, for dashboards.
Evaluate alert rules continuously and send notifications with grouping and silencing.
Keep 10-second data for 15 days, 5-minute rollups for 90 days and 1-hour rollups for 2 years.
Reject or cap series that would explode cardinality, per team.
nonFunctional: Sustain 2 M samples/s with headroom to 3×, with no data loss once a sample is acknowledged.
An alert fires within 60 s of its condition becoming true.
Dashboard queries over the last 6 hours return in p99 under 1 s.
The alerting path is more available (99.99%) than any system it watches, and keeps working if long-term storage is down.
Storage cost stays roughly flat per series by moving old data to object storage.
outOfScope: The dashboard UI itself (we provide the query API).

assumptions: 50,000 hosts and containers × 400 series each = 20 M active series
One sample every 10 s per series
A raw sample is 16 bytes (8-byte timestamp, 8-byte float); compressed about 1.5 bytes
Ingest data replicated 3× in memory; long-term blocks in object storage

steps.label: Rollup storage
steps.result: ≈ 7 TB of rollups; ≈ 11 TB total in object storage

steps.label: Ingester memory
steps.math: ≈ 4 KB per series (labels, index, 2 h of chunks) × 20 M = 80 GB; × 3 replicas = 240 GB
steps.result: ≈ 24 ingesters at 10 GB of head data each (and ~250 k samples/s each)

steps.label: Alert evaluation load
steps.result: ≈ 1 700 small queries/s, all on the last few minutes of data

estimates.takeaway: This is a write-heavy system: 2 M small writes per second, append-only, almost never updated. That rules out a general database and points to a purpose-built time-series store: recent data in memory, compressed about 10× (16 B to 1.5 B per sample), flushed as immutable blocks to cheap object storage. Memory, not disk, is the scarce resource, and it scales with active series, so cardinality control matters as much as raw throughput.

api.body: batch of { labels{}, samples[[ts, value]] }, compressed
api.note: Used by agents that push. Batches of ~1,000 samples. A retry with the same batch is harmless: duplicate (series, ts) samples are dropped.
Pull mode: the collector scrapes each target every 10 s.
The query engine picks raw, 5-minute or 1-hour data based on range and step.
Rules are versioned config, ideally deployed from git.
Mute matching alerts during planned work.

entities.name: Series
entities.why: The identity of a time series. Labels are indexed with an inverted index: label pair → list of seriesIds.

entities.name: Chunk
entities.why: Samples are stored in compressed chunks per series, never as one row per sample.

entities.name: Block
fields: labels to series to chunk offsets
entities.why: Immutable files covering a time range. Compaction merges and downsamples them.

entities.name: AlertState
entities.store: Rule evaluator memory + small replicated store
entities.why: Needed to apply the 'for 5 minutes' rule and to survive an evaluator restart without re-paging.

data.note: Samples for one series arrive in time order and are read in time ranges, so they are stored together in compressed chunks. The query side starts from labels ("all series where service=cart and code=500"), which is why each block has an inverted index from label pair to series. The partition key is the series hash: it spreads load evenly and keeps one series on one ingester. Old data is immutable, so object storage is a perfect fit: cheap, durable, no replication logic of our own.

hld.summary:
A collector on each node scrapes local targets every 10 s (or receives pushes from short jobs) and sends batches to a stateless distributor. The distributor validates labels, applies per-team series limits, hashes each series and sends it to 3 ingesters chosen on a hash ring. Ingesters append to a write-ahead log, keep the last ~2 hours in memory as compressed chunks, and every 2 hours cut an immutable block to object storage.

A compactor merges small blocks into larger ones, writes the 5-minute and 1-hour rollups, and deletes data past retention. The query engine fans out to ingesters for recent data and to a store gateway for older blocks, then merges. The rule evaluator queries every 30 s and sends firing alerts to a notifier, which groups, deduplicates, applies silences and pages people.

diagram.title: Write path, storage and alerting
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  T[Services and hosts] --> CO[Collector agents]
  CO --> D[Distributor]
  D --> I["Ingesters x3 replicas"]
  I --> W[("Write-ahead log")]
  I --> S3[("Object storage blocks")]
  CP[Compactor and downsampler] --> S3
  Q[Query engine] --> I
  Q --> SG[Store gateway]
  SG --> S3
  G[Dashboards] --> Q
  R[Rule evaluator] --> Q
  R --> N[Notifier]
  N --> P[Pager and chat]

flows.title: A sample is written
steps: The collector scrapes a target and gets 400 values.
It batches them with others and sends one compressed request to a distributor.
The distributor hashes each series' labels and writes to the 3 ingesters that own that hash.
Each ingester appends to its WAL and to the series' open chunk; the write is acknowledged when 2 of 3 succeed.
Every 2 hours an ingester writes a block to object storage and trims its WAL.

flows.title: A dashboard asks for 7 days of error rate
steps: Query engine sees a 7-day range with a 5-minute step and chooses 5-minute rollups for older days and raw data for the last 2 hours.
It looks up matching series in each block's label index, then reads only the needed chunks.
Results from ingesters and blocks are merged and deduplicated across replicas.

flows.title: An alert fires
steps: Every 30 s the evaluator runs 'error rate above 2% for 5 minutes' against recent data.
First true result moves the alert to pending; 10 true runs in a row (5 minutes) move it to firing.
The notifier groups it with other alerts for the same service, checks silences and pages the on-call engineer once.

deepDives.title: The write path at 2 M samples per second
deepDives.problem: Writes never stop and arrive in many tiny pieces. We need to accept them cheaply, spread them evenly, not lose acknowledged data, and survive one ingester dying without losing an hour of points.

options.name: Pull (scrape) by local collectors
options.how: A collector per node or cluster scrapes targets on a fixed interval and forwards batches.
pros: We control the rate, so a misbehaving app cannot flood us
A failed scrape is itself a useful 'target down' signal
cons: Needs service discovery to know every target
Short jobs may finish before the next scrape

options.name: Push from apps
options.how: Each app sends its metrics to the gateway.
pros: Works for short jobs and across firewalls
cons: One bad deploy can push millions of new series instantly
Silence is ambiguous: dead or idle?

options.name: Durable log in front of ingesters
options.how: Distributors write to Kafka partitioned by series hash; ingesters consume it.
pros: Replay from the log rebuilds memory
cons: Another large system to run at 2 M msgs/s

deepDives.choice: Use pull by local collectors as the default, with a push endpoint for batch jobs, and write to ingesters with 3× replication and a WAL instead of a separate log. Quorum writes (2 of 3) plus a WAL mean a lost ingester costs nothing, and we avoid running Kafka at this rate. Batching (about 1,000 samples per request) turns 2 M samples/s into roughly 2,000 requests/s at the distributors. I would add the Kafka buffer if ingester restarts kept causing gaps, or if several consumers (for example a billing pipeline) needed the same stream.

deepDives.title: Storing time series compactly
deepDives.problem: At 16 bytes per sample we would write 2.8 TB/day and need hundreds of GB of RAM just for recent data. A general row store adds per-row overhead that is larger than the sample itself.

options.name: Rows in a wide-column store
options.how: Row key = series + hour; one column per sample.
pros: Easy to operate if the team already runs it

options.name: Purpose-built chunks and blocks
options.how: Per series, encode timestamps as delta-of-delta (a regular 10 s interval becomes a 1-bit zero) and values as XOR against the previous value (an unchanged value is 1 bit). Keep about 120 samples per chunk; group chunks into 2-hour immutable blocks with a label index.
pros: About 1.5 bytes per sample, roughly 10× smaller
Sequential reads for a time range
Immutable blocks are trivial to cache and copy
cons: Can only append in time order; late samples need special handling
Must decode a whole chunk to read one point

deepDives.choice: Use purpose-built chunks and blocks. The data's shape (regular timestamps, slowly changing values, append only) is exactly what makes these encodings shine. It drops 2.8 TB/day to about 260 GB/day. Late samples older than the head window are rejected and counted. The bigger risk than bytes is cardinality: each new label value is a new series costing about 4 KB of RAM, so per-team limits are enforced at the distributor. If we needed many out-of-order writes (for example from mobile devices), I would add a separate out-of-order head that is merged at compaction.

deepDives.title: Downsampling and retention
deepDives.problem: A graph of the last year has room for about 1,000 points across the screen, but at 10 s resolution a year is 3.15 M points per series. Reading raw data for long ranges is slow and keeping it forever is expensive.

options.name: Keep raw forever
cons: Year-long queries read thousands of times more data than they draw
Storage grows by about 95 TB per year at our rate

options.name: Rollups with several aggregates
options.how: Compactor writes 5-minute and 1-hour points holding min, max, sum and count per series; queries pick the coarsest resolution that still gives enough points for the step.
pros: Long queries read 30× or 360× less data
min and max keep spikes visible; sum and count give an exact average
cons: Percentiles cannot be rebuilt from these four numbers; histograms must be stored as bucket counters
Detail older than 15 days is gone

deepDives.choice: Use rollups with min, max, sum and count: raw for 15 days, 5-minute for 90 days, 1-hour for 2 years, about 11 TB in total. Storing only the average is the classic mistake: a 30-second spike vanishes in a 1-hour average. Latency percentiles must come from histogram bucket counters, which roll up correctly by summing. If a team needed raw data for a year (say, for audits), I would let them pay for a separate retention class rather than raise it for everyone.

deepDives.title: The alert evaluation loop
deepDives.problem: Alerts are the reason the system exists. They must fire within a minute, not flap on a single noisy point, not page five people for one outage, and keep working when the thing that broke is part of our own platform.

options.name: Alert inside the query path on a schedule
options.how: Evaluators run each rule every 30 s through the normal query engine, track pending and firing state, and send to a notifier.
pros: Same query language for dashboards and alerts
cons: A slow query engine delays every alert
Long-term storage problems can hit alerts

options.name: Stream evaluation on ingest
options.how: Evaluate simple threshold rules on samples as they arrive.
cons: Hard to support windows, rates and joins across series
State per rule lives in the ingest path

deepDives.choice: Use scheduled evaluation, sharded by rule group across evaluators, and point it only at ingesters (last 2 hours), so object storage problems cannot stop alerts. The 'for 5 minutes' clause stops flapping; the notifier groups by service, deduplicates across evaluator replicas and applies silences. We also need a dead man's switch: an always-firing alert sent to an outside service, which pages us if it stops arriving. I would add stream evaluation only for a small set of very latency-sensitive rules if 60 s turned out too slow.

diagram.title: From a bad sample to one page
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant E as Rule evaluator
  participant I as Ingesters
  participant N as Notifier
  participant O as On-call engineer
  loop every 30 s
    E->>I: error rate for cart over 5 min
    I-->>E: 3.1 percent
  end
  E->>E: pending, then firing after 5 min
  E->>N: alert cart errors high
  N->>N: group, dedupe, check silences
  N->>O: one page with 4 related alerts
  O->>N: acknowledge

failures: A deploy adds a user_id label and creates 5 M new series
Distributor enforces per-team series limits and returns 429 for new series beyond the cap; existing series keep flowing; the team gets an alert naming the metric.
The other 2 replicas still hold its series; on restart it replays its WAL; queries deduplicate the replicas.
Object storage is slow or down
Ingesters keep recent data in memory and on local disk longer; alerts and recent dashboards work; long-range queries degrade.
Run 2 replicas per rule group; the notifier deduplicates; the dead man's switch pages if no heartbeat alert arrives for 5 minutes.
An alert storm during a big outage
Notifier groups by service and cluster, inhibits low-level alerts when a higher one fires (for example 'region down'), and rate-limits pages per person.
Samples arrive with clocks far in the future
Reject samples more than 10 minutes ahead and count them per target, so a bad host clock is visible instead of corrupting chunks.
scale: 10× series (200 M): about 240 ingesters' worth of memory at today's sizing; this is mostly a cost problem, so push teams toward fewer labels and recording rules that pre-aggregate.
Heavy query load: cache query results split by time range (past ranges never change), and pre-compute popular dashboard expressions as recording rules.
Many regions: run a full stack per region so alerts never depend on cross-region links; offer a global query layer that fans out for dashboards only.

followups.q: How do you handle counters that reset when an app restarts?
answer: Store raw counter values, not differences.
Rate functions detect a drop and treat it as a reset, adding the previous value back.
This is why counters are preferred over pre-computed rates on the client.

followups.q: How do you compute p99 latency across 300 pods?
answer: Each pod exports histogram bucket counters; sum the buckets across pods, then compute the percentile from the merged buckets.
Pick bucket boundaries around the SLO threshold so the answer is precise where it matters.

followups.q: Why not just put this in Postgres?
answer: 2 M inserts/s with a row per sample is far beyond one instance, and row overhead is bigger than the 16-byte sample.
A time-series extension can work at smaller scale, say 50 k samples/s.
At our scale, compressed chunks and immutable blocks are about 10× cheaper.

followups.q: How do you make alerts useful, not noisy?
answer: Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency against the SLO), not on every cause such as CPU.
Use burn-rate alerts on the error budget with a short and a long window.
Every page needs a runbook link; review pages weekly and delete ones nobody acted on.

mistakes: Sizing by hosts instead of active series and ignoring cardinality.
Storing one row per sample in a general-purpose database.
Downsampling to averages only, which hides spikes and breaks percentiles.
Making alerts depend on the same long-term storage and query path that may be broken.
Forgetting to monitor the monitoring system from outside.
